title: The night before the abhisheka
hook: a whole city stays up all night getting ready to pour sacred waters over its prince
carry: abhisheka: the pouring that honors the holy

segments.voice: Yesterday: a fast kept on sacred grass, and a crowning rushed to morning while Bharata was away. Your line was upavasa, a fast is staying near.

The night before a big festival has its own sound. Pots clattering in kitchens past midnight. Ladders against walls. Someone sweeping a street that was already swept. Lights going up in trees. Children who should be asleep, absolutely not asleep. Valmiki gives us Ayodhya on that night, and he takes his time with it. He wants you to see how happy the city is, so you'll feel what it loses by morning.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE A FESTIVAL.` → `LIGHTS IN THE TREES.` → `SO YOU'LL FEEL THE LOSS.`

segments.voice: Start with Rama. Before the night's fast, he goes to his mother Kausalya's rooms, and Lakshmana is there. Rama turns to him and says, in effect: this is yours too. Rule the earth with me. You are my second self. Then the city. Word has spread, and the people of Ayodhya can't keep still. Streets are sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers. Banners go up on the houses. Along the roads they set up lamps like trees of light, so night looks like day. People gather in the squares and talk of nothing else. Meanwhile Vasishtha's helpers gather what the rite will need. The word for the rite is abhisheka, a pouring: the heir is bathed with sacred waters. The text lists what's made ready: gold, white flowers, parched grain, honey and ghee, a white umbrella of state, yak-tail fans, waters from holy rivers. All for a pouring at dawn. Here's where you can still see it. Abhisheka is at the heart of Hindu worship today. In temples, priests bathe the image of the deity with water, milk, honey, curd and ghee, and on Mondays and on Shivaratri, families pour milk and water over the Shiva lingam. Same word, same gesture: you honor what is holy by pouring your best over it, the way a city once honored its prince. And all of Ayodhya's honey and holy water, in a few hours, will sit unused. Valmiki gives this happiness its full weight, so that when it breaks, nothing about it feels small. One person, though, has gone up on a rooftop, and she's looking down at all the lights.
screen: `YOU ARE MY SECOND SELF.` · `A CITY THAT CAN'T KEEP STILL.` · `ABHISHEKA: A POURING AT DAWN.` · `STILL POURED IN TEMPLES TODAY.` · then, large: `SOMEONE ON A ROOFTOP.`

segments.voice: Take a cup of water. If you pray, pour a little slowly at the base of a plant, a tulsi if you have one, or before an image you love, and say a name softly as it pours: a small abhisheka. If you don't pray, pour slowly anyway, and give the pouring your full attention, the way Ayodhya gave its whole night to one morning. Then drink what's left.
Abhisheka, the sacred pouring. Ayodhya makes everything ready to pour over Rama at dawn, and temples still use the same word for bathing the deity.
Your line: abhisheka, the pouring that honors the holy. Rama shares the crown before he even wears it. That's day five hundred sixteen.
